meta: Two children carrying wheat for Summer, a study for a lunette in Corpus Domini in Bologna by Marc Antonio Franceschini, about 1690.
about: This is a study for decorating a lunette in the church of Corpus Domini, with two children standing for Summer. A reclining or seated child and a standing one at the right are seen from below. The walking child turns left and raises a bunch of olive branches or stalks of wheat, while the sitting child holds a sheaf in both hands, its top held up by the walking child's right arm. Marc Antonio Franceschini made the study.

meta: A man on horseback drives cattle across a timber bridge over Gardiners Creek in Tom Roberts's Winter morning after rain, 1885.
about: A man on horseback drives a small group of cattle across a timber trestle bridge over Gardiners Creek, then on the edge of Melbourne. Wikipedia quotes a description of the 1885 picture as a marvelously designed view, with elongated forms made by the wooden pillars and their reflections in the water, and the bridge fence placed so that it makes a decorative rectangular pattern along the top edge. Tom Roberts painted it.

meta: Hendrickje Uylenburgh, wife of the painter Wybrand de Geest, in a lace collar and cap, painted in 1629.
about: Hendrickje Uylenburgh, the wife of the painter Wybrand de Geest, is shown in bust turned to the left, with a large lace collar and a small lace cap. A note on the back says she was born on 3 March 1600. The portrait is dated 1629 and has a pendant in the Rijksmuseum.

meta: Lattanzio Gambara's Saint Barbara with a Donor of 1558, painted for an altar of Saint Barbara in Brescia.
about: Lattanzio Gambara painted this oil on canvas in 1558 for an altar dedicated to Saint Barbara in the church of Santi Nazaro e Celso in Brescia. It now hangs on the right-hand side altar of Santa Maria in Silva, also in Brescia. It is known as Saint Barbara with a Donor, or with a Devotee.

meta: Margaret Fuller, journalist and women's rights activist who edited the Dial, painted by Thomas Hicks.
about: Margaret Fuller was a prominent journalist, critic and women's rights activist at a time when few women had professional careers. With Ralph Waldo Emerson and George Ripley she edited the Dial, a journal for Transcendentalism, the movement that stressed the unity of all creation. In 1839 she began a women's conversation group in Boston. Thomas Hicks painted her portrait.

meta: C. R. W. Nevinson's Paths of Glory of 1917, named from a line in Gray's Elegy and held by the Imperial War Museum.
about: Paths of Glory is a painting of 1917 by C. R. W. Nevinson. Its title quotes Thomas Gray's 1750 poem Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard: the paths of glory lead but to the grave. The Imperial War Museum in London holds it and calls it one of Nevinson's most famous paintings. Nevinson had served as a volunteer ambulance driver on the Western Front from November 1914 to January 1915.

meta: The bridge and town of Cava in southern Italy, a small oil study by Jean-Joseph-Xavier Bidauld, 1785 to 1790.
about: Jean-Joseph-Xavier Bidauld painted this landscape during a five-year stay in Italy, where he developed his style by making studies directly from nature. The view of the bridge and part of the town of Cava in the Kingdom of Naples has many features common in his work. He made it in oil on paper, later laid down on canvas, between 1785 and 1790.

meta: Meat, fish, vegetables and fruit with Chinese porcelain and an overturned glass, a still life by Jacob van Hulsdonck, about 1615 to 1620.
about: Jacob van Hulsdonck shows a colorful array of foods and tableware, from an earthenware trencher to delicate Chinese porcelain, an expensive luxury of international trade. The museum says the quantity and variety of food stood for a utopia without scarcity or hunger to seventeenth-century viewers. Partly eaten food and an overturned glass suggest the diners have just left, leaving insects to explore what remains.
credit_line: Gift of Janice Hammond and Edward Hemmelgarn

meta: A destitute mother rests with her baby in the snow against a pile of sticks in Octave Tassaert's painting of about 1850.
about: A poor mother rests outdoors in the snow with her baby, leaning against a pile of sticks. Gathering and selling small pieces of firewood was a common way for the poor to get by. Octave Tassaert was one of France's leading artists of the mid-19th century, known for paintings of downtrodden workers, destitute mothers, suicides and abandoned children. The museum says viewers responded well to his attention to social injustice.
credit_line: Gift in memory of Helen Borowitz

meta: Thomas Birch's painting of the Enterprise capturing the Tripoli, from the U.S. conflict with the Barbary State of Tripoli, 1806 to 1812.
about: Around 1800 the United States came into conflict with the North African Barbary State of Tripoli. President Thomas Jefferson refused to keep paying tribute or ransom to stop the pirating of American merchant ships in the Mediterranean. He sent the Enterprise to Tripolitan waters as a sign of resistance, just as Tripoli raised its demands and declared war on the United States. Thomas Birch painted the capture of the Tripoli by the Enterprise.

meta: Two elephants fight before the Mughal emperor Muhammad Shah in another version by Nainsukh, about 1730 to 1740.
about: Muhammad Shah, who ruled from 1719 to 1748, liked to watch elephants fight. He sits at his window of public audience, marked by a golden carpet, smoking a hookah, while women of the harem look on from behind painted screens. Pairs of men with fire brands and spears keep the elephants from running off. Nainsukh came from a small kingdom in the western Himalayas and painted scenes of his time at the Delhi court.

meta: The Christ Child approached by the young Saint John in Jacques Blanchard's Virgin and Child with Saint Elizabeth, about 1628.
about: Jacques Blanchard began his career with years of travel and study in Italy, going through Rome, Venice and Turin before returning to Paris by way of Lyon, and this tender picture of the Christ Child approached by his cousin Saint John the Baptist probably belongs to those years. The museum says he drew on works by Titian and Veronese that he saw in Venice for the lively poses and warm light.
